title: General Biology (BIO 101/102)
description: Cell biology, cell division, heredity, diversity of living things and ecology — the 100 Level foundation for every health science programme.

topics.title: The Cell: Structure and Organelles
topics.summary: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, the plasma membrane and the functions of organelles.

notes.b: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life (cell theory: Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow). Prokaryotes (bacteria) lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; their DNA lies in a nucleoid region and they have 70S ribosomes. Eukaryotes (animals, plants, fungi, protists) have a nucleus bounded by a double membrane, membrane-bound organelles and 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes. Plant cells additionally have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole.
k: Plant cells: cell wall, chloroplasts, large vacuole

notes.b: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins (fluid mosaic model of Singer and Nicolson). Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration and contain their own DNA. Rough endoplasmic reticulum (with ribosomes) synthesises proteins for export; smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies drugs. The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages proteins; lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes for intracellular digestion; ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis; the nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA.
k: Rough ER: protein synthesis; smooth ER: lipids, detoxification

q: Which organelle is the main site of ATP production?
Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration and oxidative phosphorylation.

Prokaryotes have no nuclear envelope; their DNA lies in a nucleoid.

Smooth ER contains enzymes (e.g. cytochrome P450) that detoxify drugs.

Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall; animal cells do not.

Lysosomes contain acid hydrolases and are sometimes called 'suicide bags'.

The nucleolus is the site of rRNA synthesis and ribosome assembly.

topics.title: Cell Division: Mitosis and Meiosis
topics.summary: The cell cycle, stages of mitosis and meiosis, and their significance.

notes.b: The cell cycle consists of interphase (G1, S – DNA replication, G2) and the mitotic (M) phase. Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells and is used for growth and tissue repair. Its stages are prophase (chromosomes condense, spindle forms), metaphase (chromosomes align at the equator), anaphase (sister chromatids separate to opposite poles) and telophase (nuclear envelopes reform), followed by cytokinesis.

Meiosis occurs in the gonads to form gametes. It involves two divisions producing four genetically different haploid cells. In prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) and exchange segments by crossing over at chiasmata; in anaphase I, homologous chromosomes (not sister chromatids) separate. Meiosis II resembles mitosis. Crossing over and independent assortment generate genetic variation. Failure of chromosomes to separate (non-disjunction) causes aneuploidies such as Down syndrome (trisomy 21).

q: DNA replication takes place during which phase of the cell cycle?
DNA is synthesised in the S (synthesis) phase of interphase.
Chromosomes line up at the equator of the cell during:
At metaphase, chromosomes align on the metaphase plate.
Homologous chromosomes exchange segments at chiasmata in prophase I.
Mitosis of a diploid cell produces:
Mitosis yields two genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
Down syndrome most commonly results from:
Non-disjunction in meiosis leads to an extra chromosome 21.
In anaphase I of meiosis, what separates?
Homologous pairs separate in anaphase I; sister chromatids separate in anaphase II.
The main purpose of mitosis in the human body is:
Mitosis replaces cells and supports growth.
Pairing of homologous chromosomes in meiosis is called:
Synapsis forms bivalents (tetrads) in prophase I.

topics.title: Heredity and Basic Genetics
topics.summary: Mendel's laws, dominance, genotypes and phenotypes, blood groups and sex-linked inheritance.

notes.b: Gregor Mendel, working with garden peas, stated the law of segregation (the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation) and the law of independent assortment (genes for different traits assort independently). A monohybrid cross between heterozygotes (Aa × Aa) gives a 3:1 phenotypic ratio and a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio; a dihybrid cross of heterozygotes gives 9:3:3:1. A test cross with a homozygous recessive reveals an unknown genotype.
k: Test cross uses the homozygous recessive

notes.b: ABO blood groups show multiple alleles and codominance: IA and IB are codominant, and both are dominant to i. Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive (HbSS); carriers (HbAS) are relatively protected against severe falciparum malaria, which explains the high trait frequency in Nigeria. Haemophilia and G6PD deficiency are X-linked recessive and appear mostly in males, who inherit the X chromosome from their mothers.
k: IA and IB codominant; blood group O = ii
HbAS × HbAS → 1 in 4 chance of HbSS
X-linked recessive traits mostly affect males

topics.title: Diversity and Classification of Living Things
topics.summary: Taxonomy, binomial nomenclature, the kingdoms of life and major groups relevant to health.

notes.b: Carolus Linnaeus introduced binomial nomenclature: each species has a two-part Latin name (genus with a capital letter, species in lower case, both italicised), e.g. Homo sapiens, Plasmodium falciparum. The taxonomic hierarchy is Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. Whittaker's five kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia; modern systems use three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
k: Binomial: Genus species, e.g. Homo sapiens
Hierarchy: Domain → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species

notes.b: Viruses are acellular and can only replicate inside living cells. Protozoa such as Plasmodium (malaria), Trypanosoma (sleeping sickness) and Entamoeba histolytica (amoebic dysentery) are protists. Fungi have chitin cell walls and are heterotrophic; examples include Candida and dermatophytes. Arthropods include insect vectors: Anopheles mosquitoes (malaria), Aedes (yellow fever, dengue), the tsetse fly (Glossina, trypanosomiasis) and Simulium blackflies (onchocerciasis/river blindness).
k: Anopheles → malaria; Simulium → river blindness; Glossina → sleeping sickness

q: In the scientific name Plasmodium falciparum, 'Plasmodium' is the:
The first (capitalised) part of a binomial name is the genus; the second is the species epithet.
Which taxonomic rank is immediately above genus?
The order runs … Order, Family, Genus, Species.
The cell wall of fungi is made mainly of:
Simulium blackflies breed in fast-flowing rivers and transmit Onchocerca volvulus.
Plasmodium, the malaria parasite, belongs to the kingdom:

The three-domain system classifies life into:
Carl Woese's three domains are Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.

topics.title: Ecology and the Environment
topics.summary: Ecosystems, food chains, energy flow, nutrient cycles and population concepts.

notes.b: An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with its non-living (abiotic) environment. Producers (green plants) make food by photosynthesis; primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers; secondary and tertiary consumers are carnivores; decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead matter. Only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next, so food chains rarely exceed four or five links and pyramids of energy are always upright.
k: About 10% energy transfer per trophic level

notes.b: In the nitrogen cycle, nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium in legume root nodules, free-living Azotobacter) convert atmospheric N2 to ammonia; nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas then Nitrobacter) convert ammonia to nitrite and nitrate; denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen to the air. The carbon cycle links photosynthesis and respiration/combustion. Symbiotic relationships include mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, the other unaffected) and parasitism (one benefits at the host's expense).
k: Nitrosomonas: NH3 → NO2−; Nitrobacter: NO2− → NO3−

q: In a food chain, green plants are:
Green plants produce food by photosynthesis.
Roughly what percentage of energy passes from one trophic level to the next?
About 10% is transferred; the rest is lost mainly as heat.

A tapeworm living in a human intestine is an example of:
